issues.issue: The stated effective date (August 1, 1997) precedes the date in the preamble, which says the Agreement is made on a day in 1999, so the instrument gives two irreconcilable starting points. Nothing says which controls or what the retroactive period covers.
"Filing of Securities by Issue (FOSBI) arrangement" is used without definition and the clause does not say who elects between segregated holding and fungible bulk. The choice is left wholly at large.

The requirement that fungible-bulk and book-entry securities be identified on the Custodian's records "as being owned by the Owner" cannot be squared with the Securities Lending Agreement, under which title to loaned securities passes to a Borrower against collateral. Whether securities out on loan must still be recorded as the Owner's is unresolved.

The record-identification duty distinguishes only among Custodian, agent, clearing corporation and book-entry system, and says nothing about securities transferred to a Borrower under the Securities Lending Agreement. Section 6 of that agreement keeps loan records separate, so the two record systems are not reconciled.

"Where the securities are physically located" has no sensible application to securities held in the Federal Reserve book-entry system, which exist only as electronic entries. The requirement therefore cannot be performed as literally written for a class of assets it expressly covers.

The permitted registration names — Owner, Owner's nominee, Custodian or its nominee, clearing corporation or its nominee — do not include a Borrower, which cannot be squared with the Securities Lending Agreement's transfer of loaned securities to Borrowers. Nothing states whether lending is an exception to this section.

The guarantee that custodied securities are "withdrawable upon the demand of the Owner" cannot be squared with Section 4 of the Securities Lending Agreement, under which the Bank has a reasonable time to liquidate cash collateral investments before terminating a loan and returning the securities. The only exception this section states is for statutory deposits under the listed Colorado Revised Statutes.

The duty to confirm "all transfers of custodied securities to or from the account" cannot be squared with Section 6 of the Securities Lending Agreement, which keeps loan records separate from custodial records and provides only a monthly loan report. Whether each loan and return required a transfer confirmation is left open.

"At such times and containing such information as may be reasonably requested by the Owner" fixes no standard for reasonableness and no outer limit on content or frequency. It also duplicates, without reconciling, the reporting duty in Section 3.

Conditioning all examination on "written instructions to that effect from an appropriate officer of the Owner" cannot be squared with Section 9, which subjects the Custodian's books and practices to examination by the Owner without any such condition. It also makes a regulator's access depend on the Owner's written instruction.

The trailing qualifier "that the Owner may reasonably request" is ambiguous as to whether it limits only clause (b) or both (a) and (b), so it is unclear whether clearing-corporation internal-control reports must be sent automatically. The last-antecedent problem is on the face of the sentence.

"Records sufficient to determine and verify information relating to custodied securities that may be reported in the Owner's Annual Statement" measures sufficiency against a report whose content is not defined here, and "may be reported" leaves the scope elective. What the Custodian must retain is therefore unbounded.

"The appropriate affidavits" is undefined — the clause identifies neither their content nor which of several Commissioner-prescribed forms applies, and "an appropriate officer of the Owner" is likewise unspecified. Compliance can only be measured by reference to a form not in the instrument.

The Custodian's indemnity for loss of custodied securities cannot be squared with Section 8 of the Securities Lending Agreement, under which the Participant assumes all risk of loss from Borrower defaults, collateral deficiencies and collateral investment loss. Which allocation governs a loss of securities lent out of the custody account is the central unresolved question.

The enumerated perils — negligence, dishonesty, burglary, robbery, holdup, theft, mysterious disappearance, damage or destruction — are all physical or fidelity losses, so whether a diminution in the value of collateral investments is a "loss of custodied securities" is unclear. "Mysterious disappearance" has no defined boundary.

"Shall promptly replace the securities or the value thereof" does not say who elects between replacement in kind and payment of value, nor as of what date value is measured. "Promptly" and "the value of any loss of rights or privileges" are equally unmeasured.

The catch-all "or similar causes beyond its reasonable control" follows a list of physical and governmental disruptions, raising an ejusdem generis question whether market or credit events are excused at all. "Laws, regulations, orders" is also broad enough to swallow the enumeration.

"There shall be an agreement between the Custodian and the agent" states a condition without naming who must procure it or what follows if it is absent. The proviso letting a domiciliary Insurance Commissioner "accept a standard of liability ... different from" the Custodian's leaves the operative standard indeterminate.

"Insurance protection consistent with the requirements of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency" specifies no coverage type, amount or beneficiary and incorporates an external standard that is not identified. Whether the warranty covers loss of securities lent from the account is unclear from its words.
